1.note: 'Growing' already implies larger in size; D removes the redundancy.

2.note: Original is a fragment, B a comma splice, D a semicolon before a fragment; the colon introduces the explained 'something'.

3.note: The paragraph presents a tentative hypothesis ('appears to'), so 'suspect' fits; doubt/fear/allege distort it.

4.note: Compound subject 'strength and angle' takes plural present 'shift', matching 'carries'.

5.note: Singular possessive of one home river; 'it' later refers to one mouth.

6.note: 'That blend' follows the sentence defining the chemical blend and sets up 'following that address' in the next sentence.

7.note: Nonessential participial phrase needs commas on both sides; B splits subject and verb, C and D misplace commas.

8.note: 'Released below a fork' must modify the fish; only B places 'those fish' next to the modifier.

9.note: It supports 'Reaching the right stream matters' by showing there is only one chance to spawn.

10.note: The sentence adds a second reason the right stream matters, so an additive transition fits; 'Even so' wrongly signals contrast.

11.note: Plural subject 'charges' in a past-tense narrative takes 'were'.

12.note: The next sentence says the sign carried news; the added example shows what news a mark could convey, which clarifies the trick.

13.note: Original is a comma splice; B makes an appositive noun phrase, while C puts a fragment after a semicolon.

14.note: B links the families' tricks in paragraph 2 to Hill's diagnosis that the pricing system was at fault.

15.note: C keeps the date and title in one concise sentence; B drops the title, D is wordy.

17.note: A colon after an independent clause introduces the list of three things.

18.note: The sentence contrasts the new weight-based charge with old per-sheet thrift; 'However' signals that contrast.

19.note: Past-tense narrative needs 'began'; C and D are wrong verb forms.

20.note: The pronoun refers to plural 'Valentines' and is an object, so 'them'.

21.note: The club history is a digression the essay never returns to.

22.note: The casual, vivid simile fits the essay's tone; B and C are stiff, D is too slangy.

23.note: The boat leans because the wind presses on the sail, a cause-effect relation.

24.note: Checking with Odile whether this is supposed to happen conveys uncertainty.

25.note: Object of the preposition 'between' takes objective 'you and her'; the reflexives lack antecedents.

26.note: Two independent clauses need a comma plus 'and'; A is a fused sentence, B a comma splice, C has an extra comma.

27.note: An interrupter opened with a dash must close with a dash.

28.note: 'Heavy' modifies 'aluminum boom' (not coordinate), and no comma belongs between subject and verb.

29.note: An adverb 'really' modifies the predicate adjective 'steady' after the linking verb 'feels'.

30.note: 'By yourself' and 'on your own' are redundant; C keeps the meaning, while B drops 'by yourself', which is the point of the scene.
